zones.label: Minnesota Climate Zones
zones.summary: Minneapolis falls in climate zone 6A and northern Minnesota in zone 7, so climate is the first design input.
facts: Hennepin County, home of Minneapolis, is in zone 6A. Northern counties such as St. Louis, Itasca, and Koochiching are in zone 7 (Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry code-change proposal).
The zone number grows with cold, from 1 (hottest) to 8 (coldest). The letter A means moist, so 6A is cold and moist (IECC convention).
Chapter 11 says Minnesota is in climate zone 6 or 7. Chapter 19 says Minneapolis lies in zone 6, so its code requirements are among the stricter in the country.
The zone selects which requirement tables apply. For values, see the adopted Minnesota Energy Code, not this poster.

zones.label: Climate Data to Look Up
zones.summary: Design temperatures and heating degree days size the heating system and frame energy targets, so designers look them up and never guess.
facts: Heating degree days add up how far the daily average outdoor temperature falls below 65 degrees F. The yearly sum measures how cold a place is (Chapter 19).
Heating equipment is sized from loads at the worst expected outdoor conditions, which come from published design conditions (Chapter 14).
This poster prints no design temperatures, degree-day totals, R-values, U-factors, or air-leakage limits. Get them from ASHRAE climate data and the adopted Minnesota Energy Code.
Northern Minnesota is colder than the Twin Cities, so both the climate data and the code tables differ by location.

zones.label: Ice Dams
zones.summary: Heat escaping into the attic melts snow from below and the meltwater refreezes at the cold eave. The cure is to stop the heat leak, not just the ice.
facts: Warm air and conducted heat raise the roof deck above freezing, so snow melts from beneath. The water refreezes at the overhanging eave and backs up under the shingles (Chapter 13).
In priority order the remedies are to air seal the ceiling plane, add insulation, ventilate the attic, and add a self-adhering ice-and-water barrier at the eaves as a backup (Chapter 13).
Ventilation is third, not first: it only dilutes heat that has already escaped, so fix the source before the symptom (Chapter 13).
Heating cables can melt channels through ice, but they do nothing about the heat loss underneath.

zones.label: Long Heating Season
zones.summary: Months of cold make heat loss the main energy cost, so the wall needs continuous insulation, a sealed air layer, and vapor control on the warm side.
facts: Continuous insulation outside the structure covers the studs, which reduces thermal bridging and keeps the structure warm (Chapter 11).
A leaky air control layer can cost more heat than the insulation saves, so air sealing is part of the answer (Chapters 11 and 12).
In winter indoor vapor pressure is higher than outdoor, so vapor diffuses outward and the vapor control layer belongs on the warm interior side (Chapter 11).
The insulation and window values come from the code. See the adopted Minnesota Energy Code.

zones.label: Frost Depth
zones.summary: Soil that freezes heaves whatever rests on it, so exterior footings go below the frozen zone or the frost is kept out with insulation.
facts: Frost heave needs frost-susceptible soil, water, and freezing temperatures together. Removing any one stops it: go below frost depth, use clean gravel, or drain the water away (Chapter 9).
Chapters 9 and 10 give 42 inches as common in the Twin Cities area and note it is greater farther north. The local building official and the Minnesota State Building Code set the value.
A frost-protected foundation uses rigid foam wings to keep frost from reaching a shallow footing under a heated building, as the code and ASCE 32 allow (Chapter 11).
Frost-protected foundations are not suited to unheated buildings or to buildings with poor soil drainage.

zones.label: Freeze-Thaw
zones.summary: Water freezing inside concrete, brick, and stone breaks it apart over many cycles, so the answer is less water getting in and room for it to expand.
facts: Water expands by about 9 percent as it freezes, and a nearly full pore can burst. Repeated cycles cause spalling and scaling, which deicing salts make worse (Chapter 21).
Air-entrained concrete has microscopic bubbles that give freezing water room to expand, and a low water-to-cement ratio makes concrete less permeable (Chapters 8 and 21).
Brick for northern climates is selected for freeze-thaw resistance, and flashings, copings, and drainage keep water out of masonry (Chapter 21).
A perimeter drain and sloped grade lower the water around the foundation before it can freeze in the wall (Chapter 10).

zones.label: Summer Humidity
zones.summary: Humid summers bring moisture problems of their own, answered by dehumidification, sealed and insulated surfaces, and a path for walls to dry.
facts: In humid summers the condensation risk reverses: cold ducts and chilled-water pipes in a warm space sweat unless they are insulated and sealed (Chapter 4).
Vented crawl spaces let in warm, moist summer air that condenses on cool surfaces, so modern practice is often to seal, insulate, and condition the space (Chapter 10).
Air conditioning also dehumidifies, and removing moisture is part of the cooling load (Chapter 14).
A smart vapor retarder opens in summer so a wall can dry, and two vapor barriers make a wall that cannot dry (Chapter 11).

quiz.question: Minneapolis is classed 6A and the far north is classed 7 in the national energy-code system. Which region shows what those labels describe?
quiz.explanation: The map shades zone 6A and zone 7, and the zone selects the code tables.

quiz.question: Which region places Hennepin County in a cold, moist band and counties such as St. Louis and Koochiching in a colder band?
quiz.explanation: Zone 7 covers the northern counties, and zone 6A covers the rest of the state, including Minneapolis.

quiz.question: Before sizing a furnace, a designer needs published design temperatures and degree-day totals. Which region tells the reader to look these up and not guess?
quiz.explanation: Climate data come from ASHRAE data and the adopted Minnesota Energy Code, not from memory.

quiz.question: Using a 65 degree F base, a day averages 45 degrees F outdoors. Which region's measure adds 20 for that day?
quiz.explanation: Heating degree days add up the degrees the daily average falls below 65 degrees F, so that day adds 20.

quiz.question: Snow melts from underneath on a heated roof, runs to the cold overhang, and refreezes into a ridge that forces water under the shingles. Which region shows the cure?
quiz.explanation: The cure is to air seal the ceiling, add insulation, ventilate, and add an ice-and-water barrier as backup.

quiz.question: A homeowner wants to install heating cables along the eaves. Which region explains why sealing the ceiling and adding insulation should come first?
quiz.explanation: Cables only melt channels. Stopping the heat loss addresses the cause.

quiz.question: Winter lasts for months and indoor vapor is pushed outward through the wall. Which region covers the continuous insulation, sealed air layer, and warm-side vapor control that answer it?
quiz.explanation: A continuous, airtight, well-insulated enclosure with vapor control on the warm side answers a long cold season.

quiz.question: A footing reaches good bearing soil but sits above the frozen zone, and it rises every winter. Which region addresses that failure?
quiz.explanation: Exterior footings must bear below the frost depth, or frost must be kept out with insulation.

quiz.question: A heated slab-on-grade garage uses foam wings to keep cold away from a shallow footing. Which region does this belong to?
quiz.explanation: A frost-protected foundation uses insulation to keep frost out of the soil under a footing.

quiz.question: Chips and layers flake off a concrete step each spring, worse where deicing salt is used. Which region explains the cause and the cure?
quiz.explanation: Freezing water inside the pores causes spalling and scaling. Air-entrained, low-permeability concrete and good drainage are the defenses.

quiz.question: In July, cold ducts in a warm attic drip and a vented crawl space smells damp. Which region offers the design answer?
quiz.explanation: Warm, moist air condenses on cool surfaces. Insulate and seal the cold surfaces, condition the space, and dehumidify.
